_bootstrapToleranceNote: The bar a configuration must clear to mint its FIRST self-baseline. A new configuration has no prior to check against, so the only available question is whether its numbers are plausible at all — and the oracle is the only reference. This is deliberately NOT the parity bar: parity asks whether the editions agree and is now tight enough (0.02 Hz / 0.01 dB) that a new port still being built could fail it, which would leave that port with no zero-tolerance regression check at exactly the moment it most needs one. Failing parity is a finding to investigate; failing this means the numbers are garbage and must not be frozen.
_gatedFftSignal: Synthetic, 48000 Hz, 0.4 s; computeGatedFFT; dB at the bin nearest the target. Kept top-level rather than inside gatedFft: consumers decode gatedFft as a map of case objects, and a sibling string there breaks a typed decoder.
_generator: HAND-AUTHORED BASELINE, lifted verbatim from the Swift/Python/web regression suites (guitar-tap-project#10). Once the canonical Swift GenerateParityOracle target lands, its output replaces this file and hand-editing stops. Vendored into each repo via tooling/sync-oracle.sh.
_selfToleranceNote: Three bars, three questions. tolerances is CROSS-EDITION parity: do the editions agree? Measured at 0.0076 Hz / 0.0030 dB on six configurations across three operating systems and two architectures, identical to six significant figures, so it is set at 0.02 / 0.01 — covering a real systematic difference (Swift's float32 vDSP chain vs float64 elsewhere, periodic vs symmetric Hann), not machine noise. selfTolerances is SAME-EDITION, SAME-MACHINE: did this configuration change? Nothing legitimately moves it, so it is zero. bootstrapTolerances gates a new configuration's first mint. One number cannot do these jobs — the old shared 1 dB figure hid sub-0.003 dB drift in the Swift goldens for an unknown length of time.
_toleranceProvenanceNote: tolerances measures TODAY'S state, and that state has known open defects — do not read these numbers as permanent or as a target. The cross-edition spread is dominated by the guitar capture path, where Swift aligns the FFT window to the sample-level tap onset and Python and web do NOT (guitar-tap-project issues #7, #3, #5). Adding that alignment to Python shrinks the per-tap back-peak deltas by 6-52% but does not close them, so at least one more difference remains in what reaches the FFT. The material path, where all three editions align, differs only by the periodic-vs-symmetric Hann window form (~1.7e-04 dB). When those are fixed the editions should converge and these bars will become loose: a sudden jump in the headroom reported by tooling/parity-report.py is the EXPECTED consequence, not an anomaly, and is the signal to re-measure and tighten again. Why frequency moves more than dB: peak frequency comes from a parabola through three dB bins, and guitar back modes are broad (curvature -0.4 dB against air's -4.4), so the fit reaches -2.455 bins/dB and a 0.0042 dB bin difference becomes 0.0076 Hz. freqHz is not an independent measurement — 0.01 dB x 2.455 bins/dB x 0.7324 Hz/bin = 0.018 Hz, which is the bar. Tighten the two together or not at all.

REG-G1._ringOutNote: Post-tap level decaying to peak-15 dB. The web is audio-clock-deterministic; Swift and Python reach the same crossing because file playback runs at real-time pace. The loose tolerance covers per-platform chunk granularity + clock jitter (web 0.0853, Python ~0.091).

REG-G2._perTapNote: Taps 1 and 7 select 296.5 Hz as Back rather than ~240.6 Hz. That is the real behaviour of the shared peak-selection path on this fixture, not a transcription slip - it is pinned deliberately so a change in selection shows up.

REG-P2._note: 3 taps PER PHASE (9 total), recorded by the web app. Each phase averages, and the peak is read off the AVERAGED spectrum - not the last tap, which is the bug this case pins. A regression to last-tap selection is what this case catches: the masked deltas were fL 0.94, fC 0.81, fLC 2.62 dB.
